new_public_evidence.source: Herbster and Warmuth, Tracking the Best Expert
new_public_evidence.result: Fixed Share supplies an explicit path prior/coding penalty for comparator sequences with expert switches, allowing the event-time proposal controller to be analyzed against a shifting proposal path.

new_public_evidence.source: de Rooij, van Erven, Grunwald, Koolen, Follow the Leader If You Can, Hedge If You Must
new_public_evidence.result: The observable mixability gap Delta gives an exact refinement of exponential-weights regret accounting and explains why a high fixed eta can be safe on easy realized sequences even when worst-case Hoeffding tuning is conservative.

new_public_evidence.source: Borsos, Curi, Levy, Krause, Online Variance Reduction with Mixtures
new_public_evidence.result: Online mixture optimization can target second moments/variance, supporting the mapping from bounded expert-advice regret to an upper bound on mixture proposal second moment.

new_public_evidence.source: Luo and Schapire, Achieving All with No Parameters: AdaNormalHedge
new_public_evidence.result: AdaNormalHedge.TV is a no-tuning shifting-expert comparator using sleeping expert copies; it provides a useful parameter-free control although it adapted too slowly in the current synthetic rare-event validation.

derived_results.claim: For event-time losses l_t(j)=H_t(j)/B in [0,1], Fixed Share with fixed eta and share alpha obeys the exact pathwise observed-loss bound H_T-L_path <= C_T(k,alpha)/eta + Delta_T, where C_T is the Fixed Share path coding complexity and Delta_T is the realized cumulative mixability gap. The usual Hoeffding eta*T/8 term is unnecessary for this ex-post certificate.

For J=3, anticipated T=300 informative events and k=3 switches, alpha=k/(T-1)=0.0100334 and Hoeffding-optimal eta=0.72972 imply a worst-case penalty of about 54.73 normalized loss or 152.03 variance units after B=25/9 scaling, too large to certify near-oracle behavior when total cumulative variance is only about 185-200 units.

On 300 held-out four-phase recurring-drift synthetic runs, eta=16/alpha=0.01 Fixed Share achieved mean cumulative variance 187.9128 versus 197.2654 for theorem-tuned Fixed Share, 215.4956 for staying at epsilon=0.6, 199.6 for all-base, and 184.5942 for a phasewise oracle. The aggressive controller was only 1.80% above oracle in this held setting.

Across 1000 independent recurring-drift runs with a phasewise comparator path fixed from the synthetic phase distributions, aggressive eta=16 had mean C/eta+Delta=1.8646 normalized units. B-scaled certificate quantiles were median 5.157, q95 5.891 and q99 6.113 variance units, while the corresponding observed-regret q95 was 4.894. Thus a large eta can remain auditable when the realized mixability gap stays small, despite a useless worst-case Hoeffding bound.

A direct event-time AdaNormalHedge.TV comparison reached mean 200.1083 variance units in the same recurring synthetic setup, much worse than aggressive Fixed Share. This is finite-sample negative evidence for this application/implementation only and does not reject AdaNormalHedge.TV or parameter-free shifting-expert methods generally.

engineering_update.scope: Synthetic 4096-branch rare-event abstraction only. Performance uses independent validation trajectories. The exact Fixed Share inequality is pathwise for realized bounded expert loss; expected true-variance mapping requires a fixed/predictable comparator path or an additional uniform-inference layer.

negative_or_scope_evidence: The aggressive eta=16 success is sequence-dependent. A future sequence with large realized mixability gap Delta can make the ex-post certificate large.
The pathwise certificate alone does not give a high-probability true-variance guarantee for a comparator selected retrospectively from the same noisy importance-sampling loss stream.
The conventional theorem-tuned Fixed Share and parameter-free comparators were evaluated only in one synthetic recurring-drift family; their broader guarantees remain intact.
Event-time learning still receives no information on zero-failure stretches.
Dependent/systematic resampling, random particle counts, environment-transition proposal bias, and real agent trajectories remain untested.
frontier: Derive a certificate-triggered epoch/restart controller that holds eta fixed within an epoch, preserves the exact C/eta+Delta accounting, and downshifts/restarts only when the B-scaled realized certificate exceeds a declared variance budget; include restart/path coding cost explicitly.

Compare fixed aggressive eta=16, certificate-triggered eta ladders, theorem tuning, and parameter-free shifting controllers under abrupt reversal, gradual drift, recurring drift and proxy degradation on independent common-random validation paths.

Investigate Fixed Share/Mixing Past Posteriors combined with AdaHedge-like learning-rate adaptation; identify which theorem remains valid when eta changes and avoid reusing the fixed-eta telescoping proof outside its scope.

Add a time-uniform confidence/e-process layer for candidate second moments so that adaptively chosen comparator/proposal paths can be related to true cumulative variance rather than only realized full-information loss.
Extend proper weighting and mixture variance control to dependent/systematic sibling resampling and random particle counts.

Build an agent-evaluation proof-of-concept where a cheap LLM judge/state heuristic guides proposal only and sparse human/programmatic high-fidelity labels define failure truth; measure label efficiency and judge-blind-region coverage.
exact_next_action: Prove a per-epoch Fixed Share bound with fixed eta and explicit restart coding cost, then implement a predeclared eta ladder such as {16,8,4,2,1}: keep the aggressive eta while the running B*(C/eta+Delta) certificate stays inside a declared budget and restart/downshift only on certificate breach. Validate against fixed eta=16 on abrupt, gradual, recurring and proxy-degradation drift. In parallel inspect public Fixed Share/Mixing-Past-Posteriors plus AdaHedge-style results for a clean changing-eta theorem, and design a time-uniform second-moment inference layer for data-dependent comparator selection.
